Although we are here measuring what we term as SOOP, there is not current validated questionnaire for this subset of SOP, and therefore the IPQ questionnaire will be used despite this minor theoretical difference.

We also collected four control measures to control for more basic, domain-general cognitive processes such as attention, and modality-specific discrimination abilities and RT, and also took into account participant age and VR familiarity into our analyses. Specifically, Balloon Analogue Risk-Taking task (BART) score (Lejuez et al., 2002), Sustained Attention to Response task (SART) score (Stoet, 2010 (Stoet, , 2017)), a visual discrimination task (VDT) score and a touch discrimination task (HDT) score. Self-reported age and VR and VR touch familiarity scores as the final two control variables. The HDT and VDT were included to ensure that results were not confounded by a participant's individual difference in being able to discriminate a touch stimulus against other touch stimuli and being able to discriminate a visual stimulus from other visual stimuli. The SART was included to minimise the impact of a participant's ability to sustain attention over a long period of time, since the main experiments involved long stretches of time completing the task in VR. The BART score was included as a control since participant's general risk taking behaviour may influence the threshold at which they were sure enough that the target stimulus was present within their environments. Age was included as people's reaction times tend to increase with age, and VR and VR haptics familiarity scores (how familiar participants were with VR and VR haptic technology on a scale of 0-5) were included as controls as participants with more experience in VR would feasibly do 'better' in both tasks than participants who were not as familiar with VR and had to learn the technology as they completed the task.

2.3 Power Consideration

Sample size estimation was based on a power analysis performed on hypothesis 1 using G*Power3.1 (Faul et al., 2007). For our study, with Multisensory Order and Unisensory Modality (not their interaction) as our two main independent variables of interest regarding hypothesis 1, a moderate effect size of .4 (Barutchu & Spence, 2021), a power of .8, and alpha of .05, the recommended total sample size is 40 participants. The moderate effect size utilised in this power calculation was based on a behavioural sensory-switching study undertaken by Barutchu & Spence (2021), since the core dependent variable (reaction time) and independent variables remain consistent with our study. In total, we recruited and tested 44 participants (19-61 years, 27 female 17 male).

2.4 Materials

Our study utilised the Meta Quest 3 and its controllers to immerse participants within a VR environment. Touch sensation was generated using https://www.ultraleap.com/ (previously UltraHaptics) HDK-REC192 touch device (Carter et al., 2013). This device utilises mid-air haptics to provide tactile feedback to users without the need for physical contact with an intermediary interface. The haptic feedback is generated through the use of focused ultrasound. The VR environment was created in-house using Unity 2023.2.15f1, with the Modular Caves asset bought from ProAssets in the Unity store.

Most VR studies which induce some kind of haptic feedback to the user do so either via controller vibration, vibrotactile stimulation via electrodes or mechanical stimulation via a glove-like device (Shi & Shen, 2024). However, each of these techniques includes the utilisation of some type of mediator to induce the feeling of touch (controller, electrode or glove). The HDK_REC192 touch device allows for the simulation of touch without the need for a mediator to be attached to the skin, providing a more naturalistic experience of what it is like to reach out and touch an object in VR. The device achieves this via a series of ultrasound generators, which work in synchronisation to project the sensation of touch onto the palm of the hand and can be programmed to induce the feeling of different shapes as well as movement.

The VR environment created was that of a cave system. In the VR environment, participants are sat in the centre of a steel minecart travelling slowly along tracks within this cave system. Participants are also embodied within this stimulation -which is to say that when they looked down, they could see their own body sat in the same position as their body in the real world (figure 2). To avoid any complications with discrepancies between the race and gender of the VR body and their real body, the VR body was covered in a brown jumpsuit. Note. An image of a participant in the real world (a) vs their perspective in the VR experience (b). Participant body position is matched between VR and the real world. The right arm of the participant is placed palm-up resting on a table in front of them, with the mid-air HDK_REC192 haptics device positioned above the centre of the palm.

Our Stimulus variable in each trial was either a target stimulus or a noise stimulus. The target stimuli consisted of one type of visual stimulus (figure 3) and one type of touch stimulus (figure 4)(since these were the target stimuli), whereas the noise stimuli consisted of three different types of visual stimuli and three different types of touch stimuli. When multisensory conditions were presented to the participant, these were always congruentmeaning that the visual and touch stimuli presented were always of the same type. In noise conditions, the visual and touch stimuli presented were also paired -meaning one type of visual noise stimulus was always paired with the same noise touch stimulus. Both the types of stimuli and the conditions were presented to participants in a random order for 48 trials in total for each block (36 noise trials, 12 target trials). Each stimulus (four total) was presented in each of the 12 conditions exactly once. Note. Visual stimuli presented to participants in the experimental tasks in order of distortion applied. Stimulus 2 is the target stimulus, whilst stimuli 1, 3 and 4 are noise stimuli, created as distorted version of this target stimulus. Note.

Touch stimuli presented to participants in the experimental tasks. Stimulus 1 is the target stimulus participants were trained on. Stimuli 2-4 were all noise stimuli. In stimulus 1, a focal point is moving rapidly in a circular motion on the palm to give the illusion of a large circle. In stimulus 2, a line moves at a moderate pace from bottom to top of the palm. Both stimulus 3 and 4 are focal points which move at a moderate, circular pace. Stimulus 3 has a larger circumference of movement than stimulus 4.

2.5 Procedure

2.5.1 Reaction Time Block

In this block, participants were told that the target stimuli they had been trained on was a species of Bat which was dangerous to humans. Participants were tasked to remove the Bat from the cave by activating an inbuilt laser system by pressing the left index trigger on the left controller. However, they were also told that this laser system could only be activated up to 20 times per day. Participants were updated on how many laser activations they had remaining through a number shown to them in the VR headset. Participants were also given a health bar which acted as an incentive for them to perform as well as possible during the task. For every unit left on a participant's health bar at the end of the task, they would receive an extra 50 pence in compensation. This gave participants a theoretical maximum of 19.5 pounds for their time (6 pounds for 12 health bar units left at the end of the task, plus the base pay of 13.5 pounds).

Before starting the task, participants were allowed to familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 30 seconds uninterrupted. Participants were then allowed to re-familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 5 seconds before undertaking the practice block, and then for another 5 seconds before undertaking the experimental block. Participants wore ear defenders whilst completing the tasks to reduce any perception of noise created by the midair haptics device.

After completing the practice block, participants then moved on to the experimental block. Once a stimulus from a random condition has been shown to the participant, the following scenario occurs:

The minecart stops moving, followed by a delay of 3 seconds. If the participant thinks that the stimulus presented to them was the target stimulus, they choose to activate the laser and their screen flashes red. If not, the participant does nothing. If the participant correctly activates the laser, they lose no units of health, but their number of remaining laser activations reduces by 1. If the participant incorrectly activates the laser (activates the laser when the stimulus presented was a noise stimulus), then they lose no health, but their remaining number of laser activations reduces by 1. If a participant incorrectly does not activate the laser (does not activate the laser when a target stimulus was presented), their health bar reduces by 1 unit. If the participant correctly does not activate the laser (does not activate the laser when a noise stimulus was presented), then neither their health bar nor their activations remaining is reduced.

Once 3 seconds has elapsed, the minecart begins moving again and the timer is reset, meaning that another stimulus will appear to the participant within a random interval of 5-15 seconds. This cycle continues until each stimulus has appeared in each condition exactly twice, for a total of 48 trials. If, at any point during the experimental block, a participant activated the laser so many times that they ended up with 0 laser shots remaining, they were told to disregard the fact they had 0 activations remaining and to carry on the task as normal.

A participant would have been told the same if their health bar also reached 0 at any point during the task.

2.5.2 Confidence Block

In this block, participants were told that they would be giving explicit ratings as to whether the stimuli they experienced in VR were the same or different as compared to the learned target stimuli (see figure 5 for a summary of key differences). Participants gave their answers on a confidence scale from 0-100, with 0 indicating a strong confidence that the stimulus just presented to them was the target stimulus, and 100 indicating that the stimulus just presented to them was not the target stimulus. A participant's score on this scale allowed us to collect both their answer (whether the presented stimulus was the target stimulus or not) and their confidence in their answer (how far from 50 the participant rated the stimulus) at the same time. Note. The difference between our confidence block procedure (a) and reaction time block procedure (b).

In the confidence block, participants were asked to rate each stimulus following stimulus presentation, whereas in the reaction time block participants were asked to react by pressing a button if they thought they experienced the target stimulus.

Before starting the task, participants were allowed to familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 30 seconds uninterrupted. Participants were then allowed to re-familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 5 seconds before undertaking the practice block, and then for another 5 seconds before undertaking the experimental block. Participants wore ear defenders whilst completing the tasks to reduce any perception of noise created by the midair haptics device.

After completing the practice block, participants then moved on to the experimental block. Once a stimulus from a random condition has been shown to the participant, the following scenario occurs:

The minecart stops moving, followed by a delay of 3 seconds. Once 3 seconds has elapsed, a slider appears in front of the participant in VR, with Same on one end of the slider and Different on the other end. The participant then rates their confidence regarding whether they think that the stimulus just shown to them was the same or different from the target stimulus. This is done using the thumb stick on the left controller. Once a participant is happy with their rating, they press the X button on the left controller to confirm their answer. Once the X button has been pressed their data is recorded, and the slider is reset to a random value between 0-100 and the timer starts again -meaning the participant will now wait for another 5-15 seconds before being presented with the next stimulus. These random values were not recorded or controlled for in the final analyses, since the random nature of the reset slider should provide adequate control for anchoring effects here.

2.6 Questionnaire

Once participants have finished both experimental VR blocks, they are then presented with a questionnaire to collect our dependent variable Presence Score and additional control variables of VR and VR Touch familiarity scores. This questionnaire includes items from the IPQ (Schubert et al., 2001) as well as some custom items. For more information, please refer to the supplementary materials.

2.7 Statistical Analyses Plan

2.7.1 Preliminary Analysis

To first determine whether reaction times in the reaction time task negatively correlated with presence scores measured by the presence questionnaire, we will conduct an exploratory linear mixed-effects model with mean reaction time per conditions as our dependent variable, using average presence score per participant as our other dependent variable of interest. We will include random effects here for ID and Condition.

We will also do the same to determine whether confidence in the confidence task positively correlates with presence scores measured by the presence questionnaire. We will conduct another linear mixed-effects model, using metacognitive efficacy as our dependent variable and presence scores as our independent variable of interest with random effects for ID and Condition.

If either of these correlations is non-significant, we will conduct a Bayes equivalence test to determine whether these results are truly negative (Stanton, 2021), thus providing us with useful information regarding the utilisation of either reaction time or confidence as behavioural measures of presence.

2.7.2 Hypothesis 1a

We will determine whether touch-first multisensory trials induced quicker reaction times than vision-first multisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. This model included Integration (our multisensory independent variables of interest with 2 levels -Touch then Visual and Visual then Touch), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects, with the log of Mean Reaction Time as our dependent variable of interest. The model also included random intercepts for ID. We also pre-registered including differences in signal conduction velocity between the visual and touch sensory systems as a control in our analyses. We were unable to find any reliable literature on this; therefore we are excluding this control variable from all our analyses. We will also not be controlling for scores in the Wisconsin Card Sorting task (WCST), since we decided that behavioural measures in this task would not capture any significant mental processes which would confound the results in our experiment.

2.7.3 Hypothesis 1b

Analysis 1b -We will determine whether touch unisensory trials induced quicker reaction times than vision unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. This model included Modality (our unisensory independent variables of interest with 2 levels -Touch or Visual), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables with the log of Mean Reaction Time as our dependent variable of interest. The model also included random intercepts for ID and Stimulus Duration.

2.7.4 Hypothesis 2a

We will determine whether participants exhibited greater metacognitive efficacy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model. Our pre-registered analyses included calculating m-ratio from confidence and accuracy values generated in the Confidence block. However, we were unable to generate these figures using the most optimal method since we did not have enough signal trials per condition per participant. Therefore, we created a replacement measure for metacognition in which we correlated accuracy on the confidence task with reported confidence, giving us a score for each participant per object per condition. We used our replacement measure for metacognition as our dependent variable, with Sense (unisensory or multisensory) as our independent variable of interest and ID as a random effects variable.

2.7.5 Hypothesis 2b

Analysis 2b -We will determine whether participants exhibited a higher overall accuracy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. We used Accuracy as our dependent variable (d' values calculated using the psycho package in R, a deviation from our pre-registered analyses), with Sense (our independent variable of interest with 2 levels: Multisensory or Unisensory), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables. We also included ID and Duration as random effects variables.

2.7.6 Hypothesis 3a

We will determine whether unisensory touch scenarios induced a significantly greater metacognitive efficacy than unisensory visual trials by using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. We used metacognition as our dependent variable, with Modality (our independent variable of interest with 2 levels: Touch or Vision) as our independent variable of interest and ID as a random effects variable.

2.7.7 Hypothesis 3b

Analysis 3b -We will determine whether participants were more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials by using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. We used accuracy as our dependent variable (d' values calculated using the psycho package in R, a deviation from our pre-registered analyses), with Modality (our independent variable of interest with 2 levels: Touch or Vision), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables and ID as a random effects variable.

2.7.8 Correcting for Multiple Comparisons

For our core experimental analyses (Hypotheses 1, 2, and 3), statistical thresholds will be kept at p=0.05 without broad multi-test corrections, as each model evaluates independent, a priori pre-registered hypotheses addressing distinct psychological mechanisms. While Hypotheses 2b and 3b share the same underlying accuracy metrics (d'), they evaluate orthogonal statistical effects (the macro-effect of multisensory integration vs the effect of sensory modality within unisensory contexts, respectively). Applying broad adjustments across conceptually independent primary models would over-penalize the architecture and artificially inflate Type II error rates. However, for post-hoc exploratory comparisons involving repeated lookups on the same data array (e.g., the questionnaire items in Exploratory Analysis 4), an explicit Bonferroni correction is applied to control family-wise error rates.

3. Results

>Results

3.1 Correlations Between Reaction Time and Presence

We first conducted an exploratory linear mixed-effects model to determine whether mean reaction time -our main dependent variable of interest for hypothesis 1 -could be predicted by self-reported presence levels.

To achieve this, we conducted a linear mixed-effects model using the log of mean reaction time as our dependent variable, with average presence score and age as our fixed effects variables and ID and Condition as our random effects variables. We found that, in all sensory conditions, an increase in presence score significantly negatively correlated with reaction time (𝜷 = -.09, SE = .033, t = -2.74, p = .006) (see figure 6). Note. The relationships between each participant's presence score and their mean reaction time in each condition during the Reaction Time task. The x axis represents Presence score, whereas the Y axis represents raw Mean Reaction Time. Presence score displays a significant negative correlation with mean reaction time, suggesting that participants who felt greater overall presence within the VR environment also displayed faster reaction times regardless of condition.

3.2 Correlations Between Metacognition and Presence

We also wanted to determine whether participant metacognition score (a correlation between accuracy and confidence scores in the confidence block) correlated with levels of presence. To do this, we conducted another linear mixed effect model with metacognition as our dependent variable, Average Presence Score as our fixed effects variable and ID and Condition as our random effects variables. We found no correlation between metacognition scores and presence scores in any condition (𝜷 = .0184, SE = .0558, t(31) = .33, p = .743). To ensure that the correlation was truly null, we conducted a Bayes equivalence test on our linear mixed-effects model. Our null hypothesis posited that there was no correlation between metacognition scores and presence scores within the predefined bounds of [-.1,.1]. The test produced a Bayes factor of BF01 = 268, indicating overwhelming evidence in favour of the null hypothesis, suggesting that the relationship between metacognitive scores and presence in our study is null.

3.3 Hypothesis 1 -Prediction a Confirmatory Analysis

We aimed to determine whether touch-first multisensory trials induced quicker reaction times than vision-first multisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model. We found no significant difference in mean reaction times between conditions in which Touch was presented for .5 seconds before vision and conditions in which vision was presented for .5 seconds before Touch (𝜷 = -.02, SE = .052, t(37.4) = -.38, p = .71) (table 1).

3.4 Hypothesis 1 -Prediction b Confirmatory Analysis

We aimed to determine whether touch unisensory trials induced quicker reaction times than vision unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model. We found that, contrary to our hypothesis, participants exhibited significantly faster reaction times in unisensory visual trials compared to unisensory touch trials (𝜷 = -.18, SE = .04, t(102.6) = -4.6, p < .001). We also found a significant positive correlation between BART score and Reaction Time (Table 2). Note. The fixed effects estimates, standard errors, t-values, and p-values for a linear mixedeffects model predicting the log of mean reaction time from unisensory touch and unisensory vision scenarios. The model includes random intercepts for ID and Duration, and BART score, SART score, Touch score, Vision score and Age as control variables. Unisensory visual scenarios were found to predict a significantly lower reaction time than unisensory touch scenarios. We also found a significant positive relationship between BART scores and reaction time.

3.5 Hypothesis 2 -Prediction a Exploratory Analysis

We aimed to determine whether participants exhibited greater metacognitive efficacy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model. This analysis found that participants exhibited significantly less metacognitive efficacy in unisensory conditions compared to multisensory conditions with multisensory serving as the reference baseline (𝜷 = -.149, SE = .0549, t(33.1) = -2.71, p = .011).

3.6 Hypothesis 2 -Prediction b Exploratory Analysis

We aimed to determine whether participants exhibited a higher overall accuracy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model. We found that participants exhibited a significantly reduced perceptual sensitivity in unisensory conditions compared to multisensory modalities (𝜷 = -.553, SE = .055, z = -10.12, p < .001).

However, an analysis of the distribution of the d' data revealed that the d' values were not normally distributed, with the data exhibiting a heavy positive skew (see figure 7). Note. The spread of d' values calculated from the confidence block, with d' value on the x axis and Frequency on the y axis. The data exhibits a significant positive skew, meaning it does not conform to the assumption of normality.

The non-normality of error terms for d' were also verified using simulated residuals, with inspection of the error distribution Therefore, we decided to perform an additional exploratory analysis by first normalising and adjusting the d' values using the following formulae: 𝑑′𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙 = (𝑑′ -𝑚𝑖𝑛(𝑑′)) / (𝑚𝑎𝑥(𝑑′) -𝑚𝑖𝑛(𝑑′)) 𝑑′𝐴𝑑𝑗𝑢𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑑 = 𝑑′𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙 × (1 -2 * 1 × 10 -6 ) + 1 × 10 -6

Once we had obtained adjusted d' scores for each condition for each subject, we then utilised the glmmTMB package within R to allow us to devise a new linear mixed-effects model which accounts for the beta distribution of the adjusted d' scores -our new dependent variable of interest. Using this model, whist keeping the fixed and random effects constant from the previously described model, we again found a significant decrease in accuracy in unisensory conditions compared to multisensory conditions (𝜷 = -.1, SE = .011, z = -9.14, p < .001). We also found that perceptual sensitivity significantly increased as age decreased (see Table 3). To verify that the model's error structures were valid, we evaluated the simulated residuals using the DHARMa package. The resulting residual plots and Q-Q plots confirmed that once the non-normal skew of the data was absorbed by the Beta distribution, the model's errors conformed to the expected distribution and free of systematic bias.

To ensure that the impact of our asymmetrical target-to-noise ratio (25% target trials) did not impact participant decision strategies and therefore d', we conducted a further analysis on the signal detection criterion (c) generated via the psycho package in R. The sample exhibited a consistently conservative baseline response criterion (M = 0.15, SD = 0.57, Median = 0.24). A linear model tracking criterion values across experimental conditions revealed no significant main effect of condition on response bias, F(5, 1050) = 1.93, p = .087, R² adj = .004. This indicates that our conservative response bias, caused by asymmetrical trial numbers, did not systematically interact with our experimental contrasts using d' as our dependent variable.

3.7 Hypothesis 3 -Prediction a Exploratory Analysis

To determine whether unisensory touch scenarios induced a significantly greater metacognitive efficacy than unisensory visual trials, we used our previously calculated correlations between participant Response Accuracy (whether or not they correctly identified or correctly rejected the presence of the target stimulus) with Confidence for each condition (as described in exploratory hypothesis 2a). Since we had 12 observations per participant, some participants were able to get over 90% of trials correct, meaning a correlation between their accuracy and confidence resulted in an error value. This resulted in 55 error values, leaving us with 121 observations.

Once we had obtained these correlations, we conducted a linear mixed-effects model using our newly created correlations as our dependent variable, with Sense (unisensory touch or unisensory vision) as our independent variable of interest and ID as a random effects variable. This exploratory analysis found no significant difference in metacognitive efficacy between unisensory visual and touch conditions with unisensory touch serving as the reference baseline (𝜷 = .117, SE = .0614, t(98.3) = 1.9, p = .06), with the non-significant numerical trend leaning toward higher monitoring efficiency in vision. However, It should be noted that the large number of exclusions may make these results weaker than they appear.

3.8 Hypothesis 3 -Prediction b Exploratory Analysis

We also aimed to determine whether participants were more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials. Similarly to our methodology in our exploratory hypothesis 2b analysis, we normalised the calculated d' variables before analysis, since they exhibited a significant positive skew. After adjustment, we then performed the linear mixedeffects model using these values and found that participants were significantly less accurate in unisensory vision conditions compared to unisensory touch conditions (𝜷 = -.032, SE = .011, t(641) = -3, p = .0028) (table 4). We also found a significant negative relationship with Age and d'.

3.9 Exploratory Analyses

3.9.1 Exploratory Analysis 1

We wanted to determine whether there was any difference in participant reaction times to unisensory or multisensory stimuli. To do this, we utilised another linear mixed-effects model using the log of reaction time as our dependent variable, with Integration (unisensory or multisensory), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control) and Age as our fixed effects variables. We also included ID and Duration as random effects variables.

We found that participants were significantly slower at identifying the presence of the target in unisensory trials compared to multisensory trials (𝜷 = .127, SE = .0334, t(179) = 3.81, p < .001). We also found a significant positive correlation between BART score and reaction time (𝜷 = .0834, SE = .0386, t(34.8) = 2.16, p = .0379).

3.9.2 Exploratory Analysis 2

We wanted to determine whether there was a difference in metacognitive efficacy between our two multisensory trials -TouchxVision and VisionxTouch. To do this, we utilised our previously calculated correlations between participant Response Accuracy (whether or not they correctly identified or correctly rejected the presence of the target stimulus) with Confidence for each condition (as described in exploratory hypothesis 2a). Since we had 12 observations per participant, some participants were able to get over 90% of trials correct, meaning a correlation between their accuracy and confidence resulted in an error value. This resulted in 42 error values, leaving us with 46 observations.

Once we had obtained these correlations, we conducted a linear mixed-effects model using our newly created correlations as our dependent variable, with Integration (our multisensory independent variables of interest with 2 levels -Touch then Visual and Visual then Touch), as our independent variable of interest and ID as a random effects variable. This exploratory analysis found no significant difference in metacognitive efficacy between our multisensory conditions (𝜷 = -.014, SE = .12, t(44) = -.12, p = .91). However, It should be noted that the large number of exclusions may make these results weaker than they appear.

3.9.3 Exploratory Analysis 3

We wanted to determine whether there was a difference in accuracy between our two multisensory trials -TouchxVision and VisionxTouch. To do this, we utilised the previously calculated d' variables which were normalised prior to analysis. After adjustment, we then performed a linear mixed-effects model using these values as our dependent variable and Integration (our multisensory independent variables of interest with 2 levels -Touch then Visual and Visual then Touch), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables and ID as a random effects variable.

We found that participants were significantly less accurate in multisensory scenarios in which vision appeared before touch than in scenarios where touch appeared before vision (𝜷 = -.037, SE = .011, t(297.93) = -3.32, p = .001**).

3.9.4 Exploratory Analysis 4

We included a final 3 items at the end of the presence questionnaire undertaken by participants which were not in the original questionnaire developed by Schubert et al. (2001). Each of these 3 items asked participants how real they felt each type of scenario was (Unisensory Touch, Unisensory Vision and Multisensory). To determine which sensory scenario participants felt was the most real, we conducted a series of paired t-tests comparing scores on these items. This series was corrected for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni correction, resulting in a significance threshold of p = 0.0167.

Our first t-test compared scores on the Touch question against the Vision question. This ttest found that participants felt that the touch scenarios were significantly more real than the vision scenarios (t(43)=5.52, p < .001). Our second t-test compared scores on the Vision question against the Multisensory question. This t-test found that participants felt that the visual scenarios were significantly less real than the multisensory conditions (t(43)=-4.98, p < .001). Our third t-test compared scores on the Touch question against the Multisensory question. This t-test found that participants felt that the touch scenarios were significantly more real than the multisensory conditions (t(43)=2.94, p = .005). A graphical depiction of these differences can be found in figure 8. Note. The distribution of ratings given to Multisensory, Touch and Vision modalities in a presence questionnaire.

Participants were asked how real each modality felt. For each condition, the median is represented by the horizontal line inside each box, while the boxes represent the interquartile range (IQR). The whiskers extend to 1.5 times the IQR, and any points outside this range are plotted as outliers. Median scores of 'realness' were significantly higher in Touch than in Multisensory questions, and significantly higher in Multisensory questions than Vision questions. This indicates that participants felt that touch scenarios were the most real, followed by multisensory conditions and vision scenarios as the least real.

4. Discussion

The broad aim of this study was to investigate the impact of touch on the SOOP in VR. We had three main hypotheses: (1) touch induces a greater SOOP than vision, (2) multisensory stimuli will always provide a greater SOOP than unisensory stimuli and (3) a unisensory touch stimulus will provide a greater SOOP than a unisensory visual stimulus. Hypotheses 1 and 3 remain unsupported, since touch did not induce a significantly greater SOOP than vision in either multisensory or unisensory contexts, but hypothesis 2 is supported since multisensory stimuli did provide a greater SOOP than unisensory stimuli. However, we also found significant findings with regards to differences between behavioural results between touch and vision stimuli and questionnaire results. Our study is the first to our knowledge to operationalise and measure different facets of the multidimensional concept of the SOOP, ranging from indirect, trial-by-trial measures of reaction times and accuracy to higher-order aspects of presence judgements such as their trial-by-trial metacognitive efficiency, and to modality-specific and modality-general global (i.e. across many trials), retrospective selfreport measures. By examining our central hypotheses on all our measures, we were able to account for the role of touch on the SOOP as a multidimensional construct.

To investigate our hypotheses, we wanted to utilise comparisons between behavioural measures of presence: reaction time and metacognitive efficacy. Therefore, we investigated whether presence scores, as measured by the IPQ questionnaire, correlated with reaction time and metacognitive efficacy. The current study found that presence scores increased significantly as reaction time decreased -meaning that we can use reaction times from our reaction time block as behavioural predictors of presence. However, we found no relationship between presence scores and metacognition as calculated in the analysis described in section 3.2. We further investigated this relationship by utilising a Bayesian equivalence test, which confirmed the results as truly null.

It is important to re-iterate here that some of our analyses deviated significantly from our preregistered protocols -specifically any analysis using either d' or m-ratio as a dependent variable. Originally, we planned to use a Bayesian estimation method to generate both d' and m-ratio values via the metadpy Python toolbox (Embodied Cognition Group, 2023). However, the parameter estimates generated by this modelling framework over our low trialto-condition ratio introduced severe mathematical artifacts. To calculate m-ratio in this way, responses must be binned into a minimum number of categories. Since we had a low number of observations per participant per condition, many of these bins ended up empty, causing artefacts when meta-d' was calculated and, therefore, resulting in the generation of multiple impossible final m-ratio numbers (negative values and values well above 1 (e.g. one participant in particular scored an m-ratio of 11.23 -1123% metacognitive efficiency). Had we used this data for our analyses, we would've had to exclude 13 out of our 44 participants. Therefore, to preserve statistical validity, we implemented alternative computational approaches. For our exploratory analysis of perceptual sensitivity, d' variables were generated using the psycho package in R, which calculates sensitivity directly from unbinned raw trial counts (Hits, Misses, False Alarms, and Correct Rejections). This was paired with a beta-distribution GLMM framework (glmmTMB) to account for the heavy positive skew and bounded nature of our accuracy data. Furthermore, because individual m-ratio modelling collapsed entirely under zero-cell counts, it was replaced in our exploratory analyses with a non-parametric index of metacognitive monitoring generated via trial-by-trial, within-subject correlations between confidence and objective accuracy. While we acknowledge this replacement measure is inherently noisier and susceptible to data loss when performance is invariant, it provides a robust window into metacognitive monitoring without forcing rigid parametric assumptions onto sparse data. Consequently, this discussion focuses primarily on the results generated from these distribution-corrected variables, while the original, pre-registered modelling outputs can be found in the supplementary materials.

Regarding our replacement measure of metacognitive efficiency, we cannot draw any further conclusions regarding the relationship between our independent variables and the sense of presence in VR. This is because we found no significant correlation between metacognitive efficiency and global presence scores. This may be for a number of reasons. Firstly, there was a limitation within our experiment regarding the gamification of blocks. Although the reaction time block was gamified, in that participants won more money for performing better, the metacognition block was not. This may have introduced a confound that meant participants cared less and therefore performed worse in the confidence block, causing our measure of metacognition to no longer correlate with presence. However, there is ample evidence in psychology to suggest that although gamification is one method to ensure participants maintain attention and concentration on the set task, it is not the only method, and other general rewards as well as the satisfaction of successfully completing a task to the best of one's ability are also sufficient (Hanks & Summerfield, 2017; Harvey et al., 2024; James et al., 2019). Secondly, previous research regarding the relationship between metacognitive processes and the sense of reality has similar results. One recent study (Dijkstra et al., 2024) attempted to define the relationship between metacognition and the sense of reality through the lens of perceptual reality monitoring -the ability to distinguish between internally generated content and external perceptual phenomena (Lau, 2019). In this study, the authors attempted to determine whether participants demonstrated insight into whether their judgments regarding the origins of perceptual stimulation (either internally or externally generated) were correct. This study found that, although participants had some limited global, task-level insight into their performance, this was uncorrelated with the triallevel insight measured during the task. Therefore, trial-by-trial confidence ratings do not distinguish between imagination and reality during perceptual tasks. It is therefore clear that, in this case, the accuracy of metacognitive judgements does not fully depend on the same signal parameters or cognitive processes as those that determine perceptual performance (Fleming, 2024). Although our two studies are underlined with different theoretical frameworks (the current study was not designed and draws no conclusion regarding perceptual reality monitoring), our finding that trial-level measures of metacognitive efficiency were not correlated with a participant's sense of presence seems parallel to findings both in the field of perceptual reality monitoring and more broad theoretical conceptions of metacognition as being dissociable from task performance. Measures of metacognition are therefore not likely to perform as good measures of presence.

We found no difference in either reaction times or metacognitive efficacy when comparing our multisensory conditions VisionxTouch and TouchxVision. This was an unexpected finding. We hypothesised that participants would react faster in touch-first multisensory conditions compared to vision-first multisensory conditions, and that this would be accompanied by an increase in metacognitive efficacy. This hypothesis was based on previous studies which suggested that touch alone contributed more to the sense of presence than vision alone (Gibbs et al., 2022), and also empirical and theoretical investigations of touch and its role in perception and action (Massin, 2009; Serino, 2019 Serino, , 2022)). Considering this research, we expected a multisensory, visuo-haptic condition in which we presented touch slightly before vision to induce a greater sense of presence faster than a visuo-haptic condition in which we presented vision before touch. However, our results suggest that this is not the case, and that there is no difference between these two conditions. This may simply be because the presentation of vision and touch together, regardless as to which was presented first, is more than enough of a sensory signal to determine that an object is present within one's environment.

In support of hypothesis 2, we found that participants demonstrated significantly faster reaction times, greater accuracy and increased metacognitive ability in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials, meaning participants felt that multisensory objects were present within their environments faster than unisensory objects. This result is a replication of previous findings in the field of human-computer interaction, which consistently find that multisensory experiences induce greater presence for individuals in VR than unisensory experiences. Multiple previous studies and meta analyses have found significant differences in how present participants feel in VR environments when the environment is purely visual vs multisensory, with participants always feeling more present in multisensory environments (Gallace et al., 2012; Melo et al., 2022; Schwind et al., 2017). Although our result here is just a replication of previous findings, this provides some validity to our paradigm. This is particularly important, since our experimental paradigm involves the usage of a novel haptic medium -mid-air haptics. Typically, haptic stimulation is deployed to participants in VR via some kind of intermediary mechanism. Such mechanisms typically include haptic gloves (Perret & Vander Poorten, 2018), controller vibrations (Våpenstad et al., 2013) or other types of vibrotactile stimulators (Hwang et al., 2024). However, experiencing vibrotactile feedback via an intermediary controller is not necessarily naturalistic since the feeling of the intermediary controller on the skin impacts the overall haptic experience. In theory, novel mid-air haptics presents a more naturalistic way for participants in VR to experience tactile feedback from objects since there is no intermediary contact with the participant's skin. Our finding that participants were faster in multisensory scenarios compared to unisensory scenarios suggests that, despite the novelty of mid-air haptics, multisensory mechanisms were still recruited when participants were presented with a visual stimulus accompanied by a haptic stimulus produced via novel mid-air haptics.

Our results also show that participants were faster at responding to the presence of target objects in unisensory vision trials compared to unisensory touch trials. This finding is in opposition to hypothesis 1. This is in spite of the fact that mean haptic reaction times tend to be slightly faster than mean visual reaction times (155ms vs 180-200ms) (Fieandt, 1956; Wang et al., 2022; Welford & Brebner, 1980). It may be that we feel as if touch confirms an object's presence in our environments due to the fact that the addition of touch to vision merely recruits multisensory mechanisms, which then go on to improve our sense that the object is present (Cooper et al., 2018; Gallace et al., 2012; Marucci et al., 2021), and that there is no special role of touch. However, there is a significant confound within our methodology that caveats this conclusion. Although our experiment attempted to attenuate the role of visual dominance in perception (Fan et al., 2020; Mayeli, 2019; Stokes & Biggs, 2014) by presenting target touch and target visual stimuli to participants in a random order, meaning they must attend equally to both tactile and visual information, it is likely that the addition of visual-only task-relevant information (the counter for the number of shots the participant had remaining, and the red health bar which indicated how many target stimuli the participant had missed) may have shifted attention, and therefore perceptual dominance in the task, towards vision. This would bias reaction times in favour of the visual stimuli. This is a clear limitation which reduces confidence in our rejection of hypothesis 1 and warrants a replication where this limitation is removed.

However, this caveated conclusion would be in opposition to the results of items on our modified presence questionnaire. When asked specifically which condition felt most real to them during the experiment (touch, vision or multisensory), participants rated touch as feeling significantly more real than both multisensory and vision conditions and rated multisensory conditions as more real than visual conditions. We first hypothesise that participants rated touch as feeling significantly more real than multisensory scenarios due to the fact that all of the multisensory conditions were temporally incongruent (vision presented either 500ms before touch, or touch 500ms before vision). We also hypothesise that this difference between touch and vision means that there is a difference between the online sense of presence and a post-hoc judgment of the same sense. It is important, especially when investigating concepts such as the SOP and SOOP, to distinguish between the moment of the original, real experience (the perception of a stimulus in VR) and the judgments based around it (presence questionnaires administered outside of VR) (Blankenburg, 1971; Jaspers, 1913). Put more simply, although presence questionnaires may give us accurate measures of post-hoc judgments of presence, they do not give us insight into a participants' immediate perceptual awareness of presence. Since the definition of presence is rooted in its impact on immediate phenomenology (Burdea & Coiffet, 2024), this raises further questions about how to incorporate other measures besides questionnaires into experiments attempting to measure presence (Usoh et al., 2000).

Additionally, it may be that differences between behavioural and questionnaire measures of presence are due to the nature of the virtual stimuli and the environment. Recent thinking in the field of cognitive neuroscience has placed emphasis on the way in which we present stimuli to participants. In a vast majority of cases, the stimuli used in these experiments are proxies of realism (Snow & Culham, 2021) -by which we mean 2D or 3D images meant to represent real-world stimuli (for an example of this, see Magritte's famous work "Ceci n'est pas une pipe" (Magritte & Torczyner, 1994)). In our case, and the case of other experiments using both VR headsets alongside haptic stimulation, the stimuli presented to participants in VR are not mere proxies for reality, but as close to real objects as one could feasibly get whilst controlling for various confounding variables within an experimental context (Singleton & Fotopoulou, 2026). It may be the case that 3D virtual renderings of objects in an embodied space produce faster reaction time measures in visual conditions because the brain utilizes isolated visual input as a highly efficient, feedforward spatial radar to initiate rapid motor choices (Gomez et al., 2018). Conversely, haptic feedback provides greater perceptual accuracy and retrospective judgements of 'realness' because interacting with an actionable, tangible asset recruits distinct mechanisms that satisfy the brain's evolutionary requirements for physical interaction and object solidity (Snow & Culham, 2021). This may explain why participants had a greater accuracy at identifying virtual objects via haptics alone and also reported these objects as feeling more real, though they were slower at reacting to them since the 'realness' of the object compared to the 3D visual-only render recruited a wider assortment of brain mechanisms (Gomez et al., 2018; Snow & Culham, 2021). This raises significant questions about how best to experimentally measure concepts such as presence as well as implement multimodal virtual environments, since presence relies on the subject feeling as if they are in a real environment and interacting with real objects.

Although we found no difference in metacognitive ability between unisensory touch and unisensory visual trials in our confidence block, exploratory analysis 3b did find that participants were significantly more accurate in unisensory touch trials compared to unisensory visual trials. This lends some very limited support to hypothesis 3, though the lack of a significant difference regarding metacognitive ability means that we should also reject this hypothesis. However, we also found that participants were more accurate in multisensory conditions where touch was presented before vision than conditions in which vision was presented before touch. Importantly, these findings cannot be explained by any subjective or objective difference in difficulty in discriminating between noise and target visual and touch trials, since these factors were controlled for in two control tasks (VDT and HDT) administered prior to the experiment. These findings to be consistent with previous literature, in that touch has been found to induce greater confidence about the identity of objects than vision in cases where the object is perceptually ambiguous (Fairhurst et al., 2018; Wijntjes et al., 2009). Since both our visual and haptic stimuli were designed to be perceptually ambiguous, it seems plausible that participants would therefore be more accurate at identifying ambiguous stimuli via touch than via vision. These findings also suggest that although we utilised novel technology to deliver the feeling of touch to participants in VR, that this novelty did not negatively impact participants ability to discern between target and non-target stimuli through touch. This provides some level of validation for the materials used in the experiment.

Our finding that participants exhibited significantly lower metacognitive efficacy and less accuracy in unisensory conditions compared to multisensory conditions is consistent with previous literature from the field, lending some validity to our paradigm. Multiple previous studies testing participant response in a variety of experimental paradigms, including reaction times, discriminatory ability and perceptual accuracy (Cooper et al., 2018; Marucci et al., 2021; Uemae et al., 2015) have found that, broadly, participants perform better in tasks in which they are given multisensory cues compared to unisensory cues. However, fewer studies have investigated the role of metacognition in incoming multisensory vs unisensory perceptual information (Kimmet et al., 2023; Meijer & Noppeney, 2023). Our finding that participants experienced greater metacognitive efficacy regarding perceptual discrimination in visuo-touch conditions compared to vision-only or touch-only conditions may be a significant contribution to the field of multisensory integration. Additionally, although we did find that multisensory conditions increased presence, reaction time and accuracy over unisensory conditions, these results may understate the true impact of congruent multisensory stimuli on presence since our multisensory stimuli were always temporally incongruent.

Future studies could address these limitations in a number of ways. First, future studies intending to investigate similar questions regarding the relative importance of touch vs vision on the sense of presence should be careful to match visual and touch dominance. Importantly, avoiding any task-relevant information which is only presented in one sensory domain. Secondly, it may be of interest to the field as a whole for future studies to attempt to decipher the role of task engagement in the creation of the sense of presence. If undertaking different types of task within the same virtual environment causes shifts in how present a participant feels within the VR simulation, this may have crucial implications when it comes to translating psychological research undertaken in VR into real-world applications.

5. Summary

This study investigated the relative contributions of touch and vision to the Sense of Object Presence (SOOP) in VR, utilizing novel mid-air haptic technology (ultrasound) to simulate tactile feedback without physical intermediaries. Across a sample of 44 participants, we employed a rigorous dual-paradigm approach, contrasting implicit behavioural measures (reaction times verified against attention and risk-taking controls) with explicit metacognitive judgments.

Our results confirmed that multisensory integration significantly enhances metacognitive efficacy, accuracy, and reaction speeds compared to unisensory conditions, independent of temporal order. However, a key dissociation emerged between unisensory modalities: while participants reacted significantly faster to visual stimuli, they achieved higher perceptual accuracy with touch. Furthermore, although reaction times correlated with general presence scores, participants retrospectively rated touch as feeling significantly more "real" than vision. These findings suggest a disconnect between the immediate, action-oriented "felt" presence dominated by vision and a reflective "judged" presence where touch is dominant. By validating these effects using contact-free haptics, this research offers a new insight into how measures of presence are collected in virtual reality studies.
